definition.text: A connection between computers or programs: a software interface through which one piece of software offers a service to other pieces of software.

facts.text: API stands for Application Programming Interface: a set of definitions and protocols for building and integrating application software.
An API is sometimes called a contract between an information provider and an information user, setting out what the producer must supply and what the consumer must send.
To retrieve information or perform a function on another system, a caller uses that system's API to say what it wants, so the system can understand and complete the request.
Good API design is a crucial part of any system, and so is picking the right API technology, such as REST, GraphQL or gRPC.

An API is a type of software interface offering a service to other software; a document or standard describing it is an API specification, and a system that meets the standard is said to implement or expose the API.
Unlike a user interface, an API connects pieces of software to each other and is typically not visible to users: it is an under-the-hood part used for machine-to-machine communication.
The calls that make up an API are also known as subroutines, methods, requests or endpoints, and the API specification explains how to use or implement them.
A main purpose of an API is to hide internal details and expose only the parts a programmer finds useful, keeping them consistent even if the internal details later change.

definition.text: A software architectural style, created to describe and guide the design of the Web's architecture, that sets constraints for how a distributed, Internet-scale hypermedia system should behave.

facts.text: A REST API, also called a RESTful API, conforms to the constraints of the REST architectural style and allows interaction with RESTful web services.
REST stands for Representational State Transfer and was first introduced by Roy Fielding in 2000.
In a REST API the fundamental unit is a resource, and HTTP request methods indicate the action to perform on a given resource.

GET requests a representation of a resource, POST submits an entity and often changes state, PUT replaces the resource with the payload, PATCH applies a partial change, and DELETE removes the resource.
A users resource maps /users with GET to list all users and POST to add one, and /users/{id} with GET, PATCH and DELETE to read, update or delete one user.

REST is simple, flexible, portable, cache-friendly and decoupled, but it can over-fetch data and need multiple round trips; it is used almost universally and is the default standard for designing APIs.
RESTful describes a system that follows REST's constraints, but the term now mostly means HTTP API design and verb practices, which have little to do with REST as originally formulated.

REST emphasizes uniform interfaces, independent deployment of components, scalable interactions, and a layered architecture that promotes caching to reduce user-perceived latency, enforce security and encapsulate legacy systems.

title: REST architectural constraints

definition.text: The set of constraints that define the REST architectural style and that a system applies to be considered RESTful.

facts.text: REST defines six guiding constraints: uniform interface, client-server, stateless, cacheable, layered system and, optionally, code on demand.

The client-server constraint separates clients from servers by a well-defined interface, with the interaction managed through HTTP; the uniform interface constraint gives one uniform way of interacting with a given server.
Stateless means no client context is stored on the server between requests, so a client that is at rest consumes no server storage.
Cacheable means every response states whether it can be cached and for how long the client may cache it.
In a layered system the architecture is composed of multiple layers, and a client cannot ordinarily tell whether it is connected directly to the end server or to an intermediary.
Code on demand is optional: servers can temporarily extend or customize a client by sending executable logic that runs in a standard virtual machine.
Applying the constraints gives a system desirable non-functional properties: performance, scalability, simplicity, modifiability, visibility, portability and reliability.

Fielding identified embedding session information in URIs as violating REST, because it can hurt shared caching and server scalability; HTTP cookies also violate the constraints because they can fall out of sync with the browser's application state.

conflicts.text: In order for an API to be considered RESTful, it has to conform to these architectural constraints, code on demand included.
conflicts.note: Singh treats code on demand as required; the Wikipedia article marks it optional, so the optional version is stated.

notes: Singh lists code on demand among the constraints an API must meet; Wikipedia (higher tier) calls it optional.

title: GraphQL

definition.text: A query language and server-side runtime for APIs that gives clients exactly the data they request and no more.

facts.text: GraphQL gives clients a single endpoint to query for precisely the data they need: clients name the exact fields, including nested ones, and the server returns a payload with just those fields.

A schema describes what clients can do once connected, a query is a client request made of fields and arguments, a mutation modifies server-side data, and a resolver is a query handler that generates the response.
Besides queries, GraphQL supports mutations for modifying data and subscriptions for real-time notifications.
Its advantages are no over-fetching, a strongly defined schema, code generation support and optimized payloads; maintainers can also add or deprecate fields without impacting existing queries.
Its disadvantages are that complexity shifts to the server side, caching becomes hard, versioning is ambiguous, and the N+1 problem appears.
GraphQL suits cutting app bandwidth by querying several resources in one query, rapid prototyping of complex systems, graph-like data models, and frontends whose needs change often.
A GraphQL server can process a client query using data from separate sources and present the results in a unified graph; the language is not tied to any specific database or storage engine.
GraphQL is not a full-fledged graph query language such as SPARQL: an interface reporting an individual's parents cannot return the set of all their ancestors in a single query.

conflicts.text: GraphQL shifts complexity to the client side and can allow abusive queries if not properly safeguarded.
conflicts.note: ByteByteGo says the client side; Singh says the server side. Both are curated; the Singh version fits GraphQL's server-side schema and resolvers.

notes: Singh and ByteByteGo (both curated) disagree on where GraphQL moves complexity; the server-side version is stated and the other is in conflicts.

definition.text: A high-performance, open-source Remote Procedure Call framework that can run in any environment.

facts.text: gRPC efficiently connects services in and across data centers, with pluggable support for load balancing, tracing, health checking, authentication and more.
Like many RPC systems, gRPC defines a service and the methods that can be called remotely with their parameters and return types, using protocol buffers as the interface definition language.

The client encodes a call in binary and sends it over HTTP/2; the server decodes it, invokes the application and returns an encoded result. Binary encoding and network optimizations are why gRPC is said to be 5X faster than JSON.
Its advantages are being lightweight and efficient, built-in code generation and bi-directional streaming.
Its disadvantages are being relatively new compared to REST and GraphQL, limited browser support, a steeper learning curve and payloads that are not human readable.
gRPC suits real-time communication via bi-directional streaming, efficient inter-service communication in microservices, low latency and high throughput, and polyglot environments.

gRPC uses HTTP/2 for transport and Protocol Buffers as its interface description language, and provides authentication, bidirectional streaming and flow control, blocking or nonblocking bindings, and cancellation and timeouts; it generates cross-platform client and server bindings for many languages.
gRPC's use of HTTP trailers makes it impossible to implement a gRPC client in a browser, which requires a proxy instead.

definition.text: Protocol Buffers is an open-source, cross-platform data format and interface definition language for serializing structured data in a compact, forward- and backward-compatible way.

facts.text: Protocol buffers serialize structured data in a language- and platform-neutral, extensible way and were designed to be smaller and faster than XML or JSON.
Message schemas and services are described in a .proto file and compiled with protoc, which generates code, native language bindings, that a sender or recipient invokes to produce or parse the data.
A schema identifies each field by an integer, and the data carries only those numbers, not field names, which saves bandwidth and storage.

Messages are serialized into a compact binary wire format that is forward- and backward-compatible but not self-describing; the ASCII text format is self-describing but loses compatibility, so it suits only human editing and debugging.
gRPC uses protocol buffers as its interface definition language, to describe its service interface and payload messages, and to encode data.

The format suits small chunks of data, not exceeding a few megabytes, that can be loaded into memory at once, so it is not streamable; it has no built-in compression and weak support in non-object-oriented languages.

title: Choosing between REST, GraphQL and gRPC

definition.text: A comparison of the three main API technologies on coupling, chattiness, performance, complexity, caching, code generation, discoverability and versioning, which concludes that none is best for every case.

facts.text: The comparison criteria are tight coupling, chattiness (how many distinct API calls it takes to get the needed information), performance, integration complexity, caching, built-in tooling and code generation, discoverability, and ease of versioning.
REST rates low coupling, high chattiness, good performance, medium complexity, great caching, bad code generation, good discoverability and easy versioning.
GraphQL rates medium coupling, low chattiness, good performance, high complexity, custom caching and good code generation.
gRPC rates high coupling, medium chattiness, great performance, low complexity, custom caching, great code generation, bad discoverability and hard versioning.
REST suits applications that want simple, uniform interfaces between separate services and straightforward caching, but may need multiple round trips to assemble related data from separate endpoints.
GraphQL is good at aggregating data from multiple sources for rapidly evolving frontends, but it can allow abusive queries if not safeguarded, and its caching is more complicated than REST's.
None of the three is better: there is no silver bullet, and the best choice depends on the application's requirements and team, so focus on the domain and requirements rather than the technology.

facts.text: API design is not just URL path design: it means choosing resource names, identifiers and path patterns, plus HTTP header fields and rate-limiting rules within the API gateway.
For a RESTful API, the path structure can follow the domain model, and semantic paths make APIs easier to understand so users can find the right API in the documentation.
Defining only a few basic HTTP methods simplifies API design; PATCH, for example, can often be a problem for teams.
Designing for idempotence in advance makes an API more robust: GET is idempotent, but POST has to be designed properly to be idempotent.
Limiting the HTTP status codes in use to a defined few simplifies application development.
Designing the version number in advance simplifies upgrade work.
For batch operations, use batch or bulk as a keyword and put it at the end of the path.
A set of query rules such as pagination, sorting and filtering makes an API more flexible.

definition.text: Returning a large dataset from an API in pieces, which handles large datasets efficiently and improves performance.

facts.text: Offset-based pagination passes an offset and a limit, as in GET /orders?offset=0&limit=3; it is simple but inefficient for large offsets, because rows must be scanned and skipped.

Cursor-based pagination marks a position with a cursor, typically an encoded string that points to a specific record; it is efficient for large datasets because skipped records are not scanned, but slightly more complex.
Page-based pagination gives a page number and a page size, as in GET /items?page=2&size=3; it is easy to use but has the same performance issues as offsets for large page numbers.
Keyset-based pagination filters by a key, often the primary key or another indexed column, as in GET /items?after_id=102&limit=3; it is efficient but needs a unique, indexed key and can be complex.
Time-based pagination uses a timestamp or date range; it suits time-ordered data and misses no records when new ones are added, but requires a reliable and consistent timestamp.
Hybrid pagination combines techniques, such as cursor with time-based for scrolling through time-ordered records; it can offer the best performance and flexibility but needs careful design.

facts.text: Result pagination optimizes large result sets by streaming them back to the client in pieces, improving service responsiveness and user experience.

Asynchronous logging sends logs to a lock-free buffer and returns immediately instead of dealing with the disk on every call; logs are flushed to disk periodically, which significantly reduces I/O overhead.
Data caching stores frequently accessed data so it is retrieved faster: callers check the cache before querying the database, and in-memory stores such as Redis are quicker.

Compressing requests and responses, for example with gzip, shortens transmission time; a connection pool reuses open database connections, avoiding the overhead of opening and closing one each time data is loaded.

definition.text: An API used in web development, defined as a set of specifications such as HTTP request messages together with the structure of the response messages.

facts.text: A web API is typically a set of specifications, such as HTTP request messages, along with a definition of the structure of response messages, usually in XML or JSON format.
The term API is often used to mean web APIs, which allow communication between computers that are joined by the internet.
Web APIs have moved from SOAP-based web services and service-oriented architecture towards REST-style web resources and resource-oriented architecture.
A shipping company's API can be added to an eCommerce site to order shipping services and include current shipping rates without the developer entering the shipper's rate table.

definition.text: The ways an API can be released: private, partner or public.

facts.text: The main policies for releasing an API are private (internal company use only), partner (only specific business partners) and public (available for use by the public).
A partner API lets a company exercise quality control by curating which apps have access to it.
Not all public APIs are accessible by everybody: access is granted either by API tokens or by customer status validations.

definition.text: Managing changes to a public API so that clients that depend on it keep working.

facts.text: When an API becomes public, its interface stability matters: changes such as adding new parameters to a function call could break compatibility with clients; parts subject to change should be documented as unstable.

A public API can declare parts deprecated, making them candidates for removal or backward-incompatible change, which lets developers transition away from them; designing the version number in advance also simplifies upgrades.
GraphQL avoids versioning: because it returns only the data explicitly requested, new types or fields can be added without a breaking change, and @deprecated marks parts of the schema being retired.
Common practice in GraphQL is to avoid breaking changes and serve a versionless API, while Singh lists its versioning as ambiguous.

definition.text: A description of what services an API offers and how to use them, aiming to cover everything a client needs to know in practice.

facts.text: API documentation describes what services an API offers and how to use them, and it is crucial for developing and maintaining applications that use the API.

It may include descriptions of classes and methods, usage scenarios, code snippets, design rationales, performance discussions and contracts, but usually omits implementation details of the API services.
It also covers restrictions on use, for instance that a parameter cannot be null or that a function is not thread safe.
Because it tends to be comprehensive, writers find it hard to keep updated and users find it hard to read carefully, potentially yielding bugs.

definition.text: The schema of a GraphQL service: the types and fields that describe what data can be queried from the API.

facts.text: A GraphQL service is created by defining types with fields, which make up the schema definition, then providing functions called resolvers to retrieve and map the data for each field.
The type system describes what data can be queried, and clients use the schema to send queries that return predictable results; the root type, Query by default, holds all queryable fields.
Base types called scalars represent strings, numbers and IDs; fields are nullable by default, a trailing exclamation mark makes a field required, and square brackets make it a list.
A query is validated against the schema before the server executes it, and the result mirrors the shape of the query, typically as JSON.

definition.text: The three kinds of GraphQL operation: queries that read data, mutations that change it, and subscriptions that push live updates.

facts.text: GraphQL supports reading, writing (mutating) and subscribing to changes to data, with real-time updates commonly implemented using WebSockets.
A query defines the exact shape of the data the client needs, and the data is returned in the same shape.
A mutation creates, updates or deletes data; it generally takes variables that pass data from client to server and defines the shape of the data returned afterwards.
A subscription sends live updates from server to client: the client defines the shape of the data it needs, and when a mutation updates the field, data goes to all subscribed clients.

definition.text: The REST constraint, fundamental to any RESTful system, that gives every part of the system one uniform way to interact so that each part can evolve independently.

facts.text: The uniform interface constraint is fundamental to the design of any RESTful system; it simplifies and decouples the architecture, so each part can evolve independently.

Resource identification in requests: individual resources are identified by URIs, and a resource is conceptually separate from the representation returned, which could be HTML, XML or JSON rather than the server's internal form.
Manipulation through representations: a client holding a representation of a resource, with its metadata, has enough information to modify or delete the resource's state.
Self-descriptive messages: each message includes enough information to describe how to process it, for example a media type that names which parser to invoke.

HATEOAS (hypermedia as the engine of application state): after the initial URI, a client uses server-provided links to discover all the resources it needs, with no hard-coded knowledge of the server's structure.
Because only the first resource's identifier needs to be known and the rest are discovered, identifiers can change without telling the client in advance, so client and server must be loosely coupled.

definition.text: An action in which a program causes a procedure to run in a different address space, commonly on another computer, written as if it were a normal local call.

facts.text: In an RPC, a program causes a procedure to execute in a different address space, commonly on another computer, written like a local call; the programmer writes essentially the same code whether the subroutine is local or remote.

An RPC is a form of server interaction, typically request-response: the client sends a request message with parameters, the server responds, and the client is blocked meanwhile unless it sends an asynchronous request.
RPC is called remote because it lets services deployed on different servers communicate under a microservice architecture; from the user's point of view it acts like a local function call.

The RPC model implies location transparency, but local and remote calls are usually not identical, and remote calls are usually orders of magnitude slower and less reliable than local calls, so distinguishing them is important.

Remote calls can fail because of unpredictable network problems, and callers generally must handle such failures without knowing whether the remote procedure was invoked; idempotent procedures are easily handled.
Standardized RPC systems mostly use an interface description language to let different platforms call the RPC, and the IDL files can generate code to interface between client and server.
Many incompatible technologies implement RPC, such as XML-RPC, JSON-RPC and SOAP, a successor of XML-RPC; in object-oriented programming RPCs are represented by remote method invocation.

Modern RPC frameworks such as gRPC and Apache Thrift add efficient binary serialization, HTTP/2 multiplexing, and built-in authentication, load balancing, streaming and error handling, suiting them to scalable microservices.

title: RPC call sequence
article: Remote procedure call#Message passing > Sequence of events

definition.text: The steps by which a remote procedure call travels from the calling code through stubs and the network to the server procedure and back.

facts.text: The caller makes a local procedure call with parameters pushed on the stack as usual; the client stub packs the parameters into a message, called marshalling, and makes a system call to send it.
The client's operating system sends the message to the server machine, whose operating system passes the incoming packets to the server stub.
The server stub unpacks the parameters, called unmarshalling, and calls the server procedure; the reply traces the same steps in the reverse direction.

definition.text: SOAP is an XML-based messaging protocol specification for exchanging structured information in web services, usually carried over HTTP.

facts.text: SOAP uses the XML Information Set as its message format and relies on application-layer protocols for negotiation and transmission, most often HTTP, although some legacy systems use SMTP.

The protocol has three parts: an envelope that defines the message structure and how to process it, encoding rules for application-defined datatypes, and a convention for representing procedure calls and responses.
A SOAP message is an ordinary XML document with a required Envelope and Body, an optional Header, and an optional Fault element that reports processing errors.
SOAP is extensible, neutral (it can run over HTTP, SMTP, TCP or UDP) and independent (it allows any programming model).
A message travels from its originator through intermediary nodes, which process the header blocks targeted at them and forward it, to the ultimate receiver.
HTTP gained wider acceptance as transport because it works well with firewalls, a major advantage over distributed protocols such as GIOP/IIOP or DCOM, which firewalls normally filter.
XML's lengthy syntax eases error detection and avoids byte-order problems but slows processing; in financial messaging SOAP produced messages 2-4 times larger than FIX and CDR.

Being protocol-agnostic, SOAP cannot use REST's uniform interface or caching and must reimplement them; verbosity, slow XML parsing and no standard interaction model led to services using HTTP more directly, such as REST.

definition.text: Hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS) is a REST constraint under which a client discovers what it can do next from hypermedia links that the server returns.

facts.text: With HATEOAS a REST client needs little to no prior knowledge of how to interact with the server beyond a generic understanding of hypermedia, unlike CORBA, where client and server share a fixed interface through documentation or an IDL.
The constraint is an essential part of REST's uniform interface; it decouples client and server and lets server functionality evolve independently.
A client enters through one entry point URL; every later request is discovered inside a response, and the client moves between application states by following links in the representation.

In the account example, a response offers links to deposit, withdraw, transfer or close; once the account is overdrawn only the deposit link remains, so the available actions vary with the resource's state.
HTML is itself hypermedia, and formats such as HAL, JSON-LD, Siren and Collection+JSON add links to JSON or XML; HAL defines links but not actions.

Fielding says the strictness of REST constraints aims at software design on the scale of decades, promoting longevity and independent evolution, and that many constraints oppose short-term efficiency.

definition.text: The OpenAPI Specification is a machine-readable interface definition language for describing, producing, consuming and visualizing web services.

facts.text: An OpenAPI Description is a formal description of an API that tools can use to generate code, documentation, test cases and more.

Applications can generate documentation of methods, parameters and data models from it, which keeps documentation, client libraries and source code in sync; generating server code stubs from it is called scaffolding.
In contract-first development the API contract is agreed before any code is written, so downstream developers can mock the server and start testing right away, a shift-left testing practice.
The specification is language-agnostic and declarative, so clients can understand and consume a service without knowing its implementation or seeing the server code.

definition.text: Serialization translates a data structure or object state into a format that can be stored or transmitted and reconstructed later, possibly on another computer.

facts.text: Rereading the serialized bits according to the format creates a semantically identical clone of the original object; this is also called marshalling, and the reverse is deserialization or unmarshalling.
Serialization is used to send data over networks as messages, store data in databases and on disk, make remote procedure calls, distribute objects and detect changes in time-varying data.

The format must be architecture-independent: copying a data structure's memory layout directly cannot work reliably across architectures because of byte ordering, memory layout and per-language data representation.

Because the encoding is serial, extracting one part means reading and reconstructing the whole object from start to end; the linearity suits simple I/O, but higher performance may call for a non-linear organization.
Serialization breaks the opacity of an abstract data type by potentially exposing private implementation details, and naive implementations that serialize all data members may violate encapsulation.
Interoperability requires that applications understand each other's serialization formats, so remote method call architectures such as CORBA define their serialization formats in detail.
Some language serializers are unsafe with untrusted input: Python's pickle is not secure against erroneous or malicious data, and PHP's unserialize() is often dangerous on completely untrusted data.

definition.text: Serialization formats range from compact binary encodings such as XDR to human-readable text encodings such as XML, JSON and YAML.

facts.text: Sun's External Data Representation (XDR), published in 1987, is an open binary format standardized as RFC 4506.

XML gave a human-readable text encoding useful for objects that humans read or that other systems consume regardless of language; it loses the compact byte-stream encoding, which mattered less once storage and transmission capacity grew.
JSON is a lightweight plain-text alternative to XML, commonly used for client-server communication in web applications, independent of JavaScript and standardized as RFC 8259.
YAML is a strict superset of JSON that adds data type tags, cyclic data structures, indentation-sensitive syntax and several forms of scalar quoting.
Large scientific datasets use specific binary serialization standards such as HDF, netCDF and GRIB.
Avro, from Hadoop, serves as a format for persistent data and as a wire format, with binary and JSON encodings; unlike Protocol Buffers it needs no code generation when a schema changes.
